# Project Summary {.unnumbered}

Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) control depends on finding aggregations before they consume substantial coral. Project CCIP-BR-13 combined fine-scale habitat maps, operational observations, hydrodynamic and connectivity modelling, and a prototype population model to guide searches within reefs and compare control across connected reefs. It addressed the program's Detection & Monitoring and Decisions for Coral Resilience priorities.

The generated habitat maps cover the Great Barrier Reef at 30 m resolution, but provide only weak rankings on their own. Adding recent cull and manta observations improved cull-site selection. Deferring the lowest-ranked 20% of sites retained `r p1(oc("high_retained"))` of observed dives above 0.04 COTS per minute of bottom time, against `r p1(oc("high_retained", "random"))` for random sites, but avoided no more low-density or empty dives than random selection.

Building on GBRMPA's analysis of feeding-scar triggers, the ranking was translated into an on-water workflow. Crews still dive open sites and sites near strong manta evidence; only the remaining dives are ranked. The 5 November 2026 delivery workshop led to density-aware priority classes, which reflect each reef's recent density and each site's own record, and to shaded exploration zones of rarely searched habitat. Replayed on 2020–2026 records, diving those remaining sites only in classes A–D avoided `r p1(crv("ghost_avoided_pct"))` of empty dives and missed `r p1(crv("high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04; skipping the same number at random avoided `r p1(crd("ghost_avoided_pct"))` and missed `r p1(crd("high_missed_pct"))`. Towing only the A–C zone on follow-up visits saved `r p0(ccv("tows_saved_follow_up_pct"))` of those tows. Habitat-only tow selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning.

Products include a 2027 ranking of `r int(n_sites)` cull sites and reproducible workflows. The COTS–coral model, integrated with AIMS's ADRIA framework, reproduces historical irruption patterns and supports exploratory scenarios through 2050. On two reefs outside its calibration it placed past irruption peaks within two years, but density mismatches, full validation and an assessment of control since 2012 remain outstanding.

Intended benefits, still to be measured, are less crew time on empty dives, more search of overlooked habitat and better protection of coral for Reef communities. GBRMPA meetings guided delivery, Malu engagement supported a future Far Northern model, and vessel trials are planned for January–February 2027.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Context & Objectives

## The management problem

Irruptions of crown-of-thorns starfish (*Acanthaster* cf. *solaris*; COTS) are a major cause of coral loss on the Great Barrier Reef [@death2012decline; @pratchett2017thirty]. The COTS Control Program suppresses irruptions by manual culling, which can protect coral when sustained at the right reefs [@matthews2024protecting]. A substantial portion of operational effort goes into searching for COTS, creating opportunities to improve where surveillance and culling are directed.

Manta tow surveillance records COTS and feeding scars and assesses reef irruption status. Crews then choose cull sites using manta results and previous culling records. The current EoTR register contains `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs, of which approximately 1,300 sites across 200 actioned reefs are typically culled each year [@gbrmpadashboard2026]. The dashboards bring together recent observations to support these decisions [@matthews2025intelligence]. In the held-out cull records from 2018 to 2026, `r p0(cs_ghost / cs_dives)` of dives found no COTS (ghost dives), and a further `r p0(cs_low / cs_dives)` found COTS at CPUE below 0.02 COTS per minute of bottom time (low-density dives).
<!-- Approximate annual site/reef activity supplied by the author in review 02,
with the COTS Dashboard as source. Confirm reporting period for the approximate
1,300-site figure before finalisation; register totals remain inline results. -->

The operational strategy links decisions from individual sites to voyages and regional priorities [@fletcher2020strategy]. In practice, tow routes mostly follow established cull sites around reef perimeters. Many sites were initially delineated from satellite maps in 2018, leaving gaps in lagoon bommie fields, shallow crests and isolated patches. Search can therefore repeatedly trigger dives where few COTS are found while overlooking other potential habitat. Reducing repeated searches in low-priority areas could free effort to search these gaps, improving both efficiency and the chance of finding previously undetected populations.
<!-- Current practice and the history of site delineation supplied by the author
in review 02; Fletcher supports the operational framework, not these specific
observations about the current site register. -->

Crews and GBRMPA analysts already hold useful information about recent culling, empty sites, and COTS or scars seen on manta tows. This knowledge is strongest on frequently visited reefs and within the established search footprint. Fine-scale habitat maps cover places with little recent evidence, including potential search areas outside that footprint, but say little about whether COTS are present this season. This project combines these sources to prioritise familiar sites and identify additional places to search.

## Earlier models this project builds on

Most COTS modelling has treated whole reefs as its spatial units, either across the GBR for regional planning [@condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative; @matthews2020cotsmod] or on individual reefs to inform culling thresholds [@morello2014model; @plaganyi2020targets]. Reef-level species distribution models (SDMs), which relate species observations to environmental conditions, showed that larval connectivity and water quality explain much of the spatial distribution of irruptions [@matthews2020connectivity], and a hybrid machine-learning model estimates each reef's annual irruption probability [@stewart2026hybrid]. Population and ecosystem models help compare regional control strategies and ecological targets, but their whole-reef units do not identify where within a reef to search or cull.

Recent developments support finer spatial resolution. Coral species distribution models use satellite-derived multiscale terrain and benthic variables to map habitat for key coral taxa at tens of metres [@guillaume2025coral]. Their predictions and environmental predictors are inputs to the habitat modelling here, which maps COTS suitability at 30 m and combines it with recent program observations.

In parallel, advances in hydrodynamic and COTS larval-connectivity modelling provide a route to representing connections among smaller areas of reef. This project adapts COTSMod, a spatially explicit model of COTS populations and coral recovery [@matthews2020cotsmod], to represent site-level dynamics in the northern GBR irruption initiation box. It uses AIMS's high-throughput ADRIA ecosystem modelling framework and CoralBlox coral dynamics [@adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. The prototype covers the Lizard Island cluster, with 2,895 sub-reef sites on 113 reefs. Its present transport inputs remain at reef scale; the fine-scale hydrodynamic network has not yet replaced them. This distinction matters when interpreting its capacity to represent within-reef differences ([the population-model Methods](#sec-metacommunity)).

## The decisions this work supports

The tactical work addresses two operational uses: reducing manta tow effort while retaining detection of COTS aggregations, and searching fewer cull sites while avoiding empty or low-density dives. For management, the priority is to retain dives above 0.04 COTS per minute of bottom time. Missing some dives between 0.02 and 0.04 is acceptable under the proposed operational decision criterion; these should not carry the same penalty as missed dives above 0.04. The 0.04 value is the management target used here, while ecological sustainability also depends on coral cover [@plaganyi2020targets; @gbrmpadashboard2026]. The existing retrospective analyses used ≥0.02 to define a problematic dive and <0.02 for a low-density dive. Those results are retained under their original definitions, alongside a separate evaluation of the unchanged rankings against the >0.04 management criterion ([the cull-site Results](#sec-high-density)).

Reducing search effort can miss COTS even when sites are dropped without a model. The evaluation therefore asks whether a ranking finds more aggregations or retains more high-density dives than random selection at the same effort. For manta surveillance, it also compares model selection with evenly spaced tows. These comparisons distinguish the value of the ranking from the saving achieved simply by searching less. Additional searches outside the familiar footprint address a separate question: whether effort released from repeat searches can improve coverage and detection elsewhere.

Retrospective site selection does not describe how crews decide on the water. They dive open sites first, those whose last dive exceeded 0.04, and then sites near manta tows that show COTS or feeding scars. GBRMPA's own ad hoc analysis of these triggers, prompted by managers' needs and crew knowledge, led the program to count feeding scars rather than record them only as absent, present or common. It suggested that requiring at least two scars before diving could reduce empty dives, but might miss too many sites above 0.04. That question was outside the original objectives. It became the starting point for translating the ranking into a proposed on-water workflow that keeps the existing triggers and uses the ranking only for dives on weaker evidence ([the workflow Discussion](#sec-workflow)).
<!-- GBRMPA ad hoc scar analysis: described by the author in chat, 2 November
2026. No document to cite; framed as a response to managers' needs and their
own knowledge. -->

A strategic decision sits above these: how to allocate control among connected reefs in a cluster or region. When should culling stop on a heavily affected reef if its remaining coral cannot be protected? When should control continue on a reef whose COTS population cannot be brought below a local target, because reducing its larval export could protect other reefs? A site-level model of population growth, collapse, dispersal and coral consumption is needed to compare those consequences. Evidence of renewed population growth at Lizard Island [@chandler2023densities; @uthicke2024edna] also motivates assessing whether the emerging fifth primary irruption wave can be suppressed, and what resources this would require.

## Project priorities and objectives

The Work Plan identifies Decisions for Coral Resilience and Detection & Monitoring as the priority research areas. The bridging project adapts coral-habitat and hydrodynamic capabilities developed through linked NESP and RRAP work to COTS decisions, rather than duplicating those investments. The habitat and search evaluations address tactical planning; the Lizard Island prototype establishes the basis for strategic tests. Appendix A maps the Work Plan outputs to the evidence and remaining development needs.

The specific project objectives were to:

- Develop GBR-wide predictive fine-scale habitat suitability models by connecting fine-scale COTS data to new high-resolution benthic and coral habitat data.
- Optimise and standardise surveillance paths to improve irruption detection and operational efficiency, including a comparison against traditional perimeter-based surveillance.
- Refine site-level management strategies for individual reefs through predicted suitable habitat and metapopulation modelling.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Methods

## Observations and habitat information

The analyses used existing Control Program and monitoring records across the GBR. Cull records covered 2002–2026; after excluding missing catches and invalid bottom time, matched records represented `r int(crscope$matched_sites)` designated sites on `r int(crscope$matched_reefs)` reefs. Catch per unit effort (CPUE) was COTS culled per minute of bottom time. Ghost dives found no COTS; low-density dives had positive CPUE <0.02. Models were fitted to CPUE ≥0.02. Rankings were then assessed, without refitting, against dives strictly above 0.04, the program's ecological target where coral cover is below 40% [@plaganyi2020targets; @gbrmpadashboard2026]. Dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive formed an intermediate group.

Manta tows supplied COTS sightings and feeding-scar observations. Strong evidence meant a direct sighting, at least two counted scars, or scars recorded as common in legacy surveys. Scooter-assisted large area diver-based surveys and Reef Health and Impact Surveys contributed to the explanatory habitat model [@pratchett2022salad; @beeden2014rhis], and ReefScan sightings supplied a separate presence-only check [@bainbridge2024reefscan]. Habitat predictors described depth, seabed shape, exposure, turbidity and predicted habitat for three *Acropora* taxa at 30 m resolution [@guillaume2025coral; @reefguide2026; @gbrmpabathymetry2021; @gbrmpageomorphic2021; @roelfsema2021shallow] (Appendix B). No new sampling of COTS or coral was undertaken for these model fits. [TO CONFIRM: relevant approvals and permits governing reuse of the source observations.]

@fig-study-area locates the available cull observations for habitat modelling, the northern population-model calibration reefs and the model's sub-reef domain.

![Study areas and observations. A: reef locations with georeferenced cull records in the archived 2002–2026 data, available for habitat modelling; symbols summarise locations by reef. B: Lizard Island, Eyrie, MacGillivray and North Direction, whose monitoring series informed population-model calibration. C: reserved for the hydrodynamic mesh figure, to be supplied. D: the 2,895 sub-reef polygons on 113 reefs in the population model's v0.4 GeoPackage. The panels describe data and model support, not independent validation or new fieldwork. Fine-scale hydrodynamic transport has not yet replaced the population model's reef-level connections.](../outputs/figures/fig29_report_study_area.png){#fig-study-area width="100%"}

## Testing habitat and recent-evidence rankings

Each designated site's score combined its within-reef habitat rank with the preceding season's cull and nearby manta evidence through a logistic regression fitted to dive outcomes (Appendix B). The score therefore encodes crew behaviour as well as habitat. Sites were ordered on each reef and assigned classes A (top 20%), B (to 50%), C (to 66%), D (to 80%) and E (the remainder).

All designated sites were candidates, including never-dived sites, whose outcomes remain unknown. Evaluation used habitat fits that withheld each reef's group and, for 2019–2026, evidence regressions fitted only on earlier seasons. Rankings were compared with random selection at the same site count and at matched retention of dives above 0.04, and manta thinning was also compared with evenly spaced tows. Uncertainty resampled whole reef-years. Appendices B and C give the evaluation design, tow-effort estimates and three pre-specified alternative rankings.

## Replaying a proposed on-water workflow {#sec-workflow-methods}

A further analysis, developed with GBRMPA after the original objectives were set, replayed a proposed workflow on recorded reef visits with a manta survey in the 30 days before or during culling: `r int(ptot$visits)` visits, `r int(ptot$dives)` dives at designated sites and `r int(ptot$tows)` tows in 2019–2026. Open sites, whose last dive in the previous 365 days exceeded 0.04, and sites within 100 m of a strong-evidence tow were dived as now. The ranking, refreshed to each voyage's departure, decided only the remaining dives. On follow-up visits, later visits to a reef in the same season, tows were restricted to a zone of higher-ranked sites, open sites and sites near strong tows earlier that season. A dive whose only nearby strong tows were skipped counted as missed. Baselines skipped the same number of dives at random among those without strong evidence, and the same tows at other positions or as blocks of nine tows on and three off.

Within-reef classes give every reef the same shares of sites, however many COTS it holds. Density-aware classes, developed after the 5 November 2026 delivery workshop, let those shares move with reef density. Density-aware v2, the chosen product, estimates a reef's density from its dives and tows weighted by a 90-day half-life, including tow-only surveys. Each site's class then comes from that density and the site's own record; reefs without recent evidence keep density quotas. Class cut-offs give the same pooled shares of sites as the within-reef classes. Each version was replayed strictly forward over 2020–2026, refitted on earlier seasons, and compared at matched effort (Appendix D).

## Seasonal search products

The 2027 ranking used the latest available 12 months, June 2025–May 2026. Exploration zones, which replaced an earlier set of discrete areas after the workshop, shade high-ranked habitat outside designated sites and away from recent tow paths, as nested bands of the reef's top 40, 30, 20 and 10% of habitat (@fig-2027).

![Batt Reef and Eyrie Reef: 2027 density-aware v2 cull-site priority, manta tows of the last five seasons (blue) and exploration zones (purple; darker is better-ranked habitat) over satellite imagery. Class shares vary among reefs with their density. The recommended workflow tows the A–C zone on follow-up visits and makes dives without strong evidence only at A–D sites. These maps illustrate the rules, rather than showing measured performance at Batt or Eyrie in 2027.](../outputs/figures/fig17_search_2027_exploration.png){#fig-2027 width="100%"}

## Water movement and larval connections {#sec-hydro-connectivity-methods}

A three-dimensional COMPAS–EMS model of the far northern GBR, nested within the 4 km eReefs model, simulated circulation from 20 November 2022 to 1 April 2023. Particles released across potential COTS habitat on ten dates were tracked for 45 days. Daily mean concentrations at larval ages 5, 9 and 10 days were ranked within each of the `r int(lc_scope$releases)` releases, which describes relative exposure rather than origins or settlement. The tracks were also combined with fitted larval survival and competency functions to estimate connectivity among sub-reefs [@stewart2026dispersal]. Matrix results are pending and are not reported here (Appendix E).

## Connected COTS and coral populations {#sec-metacommunity}

The Lizard Island prototype represents `r int(lc_scope$sites)` sites on `r int(lc_scope$reefs)` reefs. COTSMod supplies population stages, predation and larval processes; ADRIA handles the spatial domain and disturbances, coupled to CoralBlox coral dynamics [@matthews2020cotsmod; @cotsmodmethods2026; @adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. Transport remains reef-to-reef. Calibration compared irruption timing, size, troughs and coral change on four monitoring reefs. Five further monitoring reefs outside the calibration score were then compared with their manta records. Initial projections linked diver-hours to removals and compared control effort through 2050 (Appendix E).

## Engagement with Rights-holders and Management Stakeholders {#sec-engagement}

GBRMPA meetings throughout the project guided delivery, including the decision to rank designated cull sites. Earlier informal feedback also informed map formats, uncertainty communication and integration with existing planning systems. The progress report records November discussions with Malu Ventures and Jabalbina about interpretation and operator use. Engagement with Malu included an April 2026 visit and June follow-up. Fine-scale observations were collected for a standalone Far Northern species distribution model planned for future development; they were not used to fit the models assessed here.

The delivery workshop on 5 November 2026 led directly to the density-aware classes and to replacing discrete exploration areas with shaded zones. [TO CONFIRM: workshop participants.] Trials of the density-aware v2 ranking, dive rule and tow zone are planned aboard BPM in Cairns and with Malu in the Far Northern GBR and Torres Strait during January–February 2027. They will compare the recommendations with crew practice and record detection, effort and follow-up at deferred sites.

# Results

## GBR fine-scale habitat predictions {#sec-cull}

### Habitat layers give a consistent but weak first ordering {.unnumbered}

The habitat layers provide a first search order across the GBR, including reefs with little recent evidence (@fig-maps). On their own, they discriminate only modestly between places on the same reef. On independent manta tows, the limited-extent habitat model reached a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(mi("RG + year", "within_reef_year_auc"), mi("RG + year", "auc_low"), mi("RG + year", "auc_high"))` (@tbl-manta). The manta model, trained on tows but scored leave-reef-out, reached `r ci3(mt("within", "auc"), mt("within", "auc", "low"), mt("within", "auc", "high"))`.

![Within-reef habitat ranks on Eyrie, Batt, Broadhurst and Lady Musgrave reefs. Columns show the full-extent and limited-extent cull-trained models, the manta-trained model, the joint habitat model, habitat updated with cull history for 2027, and joint-model uncertainty (90% posterior interval width). The top 30% of each reef is emphasised. Satellite imagery: Esri World Imagery; full attribution is in Appendix C.](../outputs/figures/fig02b_four_reef_comparison_imagery.png){#fig-maps width="100%"}

### Recent evidence improves cull-site selection {#sec-high-density}

Combining recent cull and manta observations with habitat improved on habitat alone. Over 2019–2026 (`r int(fw_dives)` dives in `r int(fw_ry)` reef-years), retaining 90% of dives above 0.04 required selecting `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.9)` of designated sites, against `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.9, "habitat"))` for habitat alone and `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.9, "random"))` at random. Deferring class E on every reef retained `r occi("high_retained")` of those dives, against `r occi("high_retained", "random")` for the same number of random sites. It did not avoid more unproductive dives than random selection: it avoided `r p1(oc("low_avoided"))` of low-density and `r p1(oc("ghost_avoided"))` of ghost dives, against `r p1(oc("low_avoided", "random"))` and `r p1(oc("ghost_avoided", "random"))`. Its benefit is protecting productive dives (Appendix C).

Savings against random selection are not savings against current practice. Open sites, which crews already dive first, held `r p0(mzp("open", "high") / ptot$high)` of dives above 0.04. The workflow replay below is the fairer test. Habitat's main practical role is coverage: `r p0(n_noev / nrow(pri))` of designated sites in the 2027 product were on reefs without dives or tows in the preceding 12 months. A recent-CPUE alternative showed modest gains whose paired interval was uncertain, and it was not adopted ([Appendix C](#sec-ranking-alternatives)).

### Ranking only weak-evidence dives avoids more empty dives {#sec-workflow-results}

On the same `r int(ptot$visits)` visits, applying the within-reef ranking only to dives without strong evidence, at A–C, skipped a similar share of dives to the site rule (`r p1(ps(WF, "dives_avoided_pct"))` against `r p1(ps(SR, "dives_avoided_pct"))`). It missed `r psci(WF, "high_missed_pct")` of dives above 0.04, against `r psci(SR, "high_missed_pct")`, and avoided `r p1(ps(WF, "ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives, against `r p1(ps(SR, "ghost_avoided_pct"))`. Most ghost dives followed weak evidence: `r p0(mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "ghost") / ptot$ghost)` were at sites whose nearest tows showed at most a single scar. Simply not diving on weak evidence, the two-scar trigger considered by GBRMPA, avoided `r p0(ps("evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives", "ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives but missed `r p1(ps("evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives", "high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04. The ranking's contribution was choosing which of those dives to skip.

### Density-aware classes and the recommended settings {.unnumbered}

Density-aware classes improved this trade-off on 2020–2026 visits. Where 3% of dives above 0.04 were missed, density-aware v2 avoided `r p1(dlmv(V2, "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"))` of ghost dives, against `r p1(dlmv("density-aware", "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"))` for the first density-aware version (`r dlmd(V2, "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed")`) and `r p1(dlmv("within-reef", "ghost_avoided_at_3pct_missed"))` for within-reef classes. The weight on one of v2's site models was chosen on these test seasons, so this margin is somewhat optimistic.

The recommended settings use v2 with a dive rule at A–D and a follow-up tow zone at A–C (@tbl-workflow-headline). The dive rule avoided `r cri("ghost_avoided_pct")` of ghost and `r p1(crv("low_avoided_pct"))` of low-density dives, and missed `r cri("high_missed_pct")` of dives above 0.04. Skipping the same number at random avoided `r p1(crd("ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives and missed `r p1(crd("high_missed_pct"))`. Each dive above 0.04 missed came with `r num(crv("ghost_per_high_missed"), 1)` ghost dives avoided, against `r num(crd("ghost_per_high_missed"), 1)` at random. Rules based on tow evidence alone did no better than random (Appendix D). With the tow zone added, the recommended settings missed `r int(ccv("high_missed"))` dives above 0.04 (`r p1(ccv("high_missed_pct"))`) over seven seasons.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-workflow-headline
#| tbl-cap: "The site rule and dive rules compared. Percentages [95% reef-year bootstrap intervals]. The site rule uses within-reef classes on 2019–2026 visits; other rows are forward replays of 2020–2026 visits. Dive rules apply only to dives without strong evidence; the random row skips the same number of those dives as the v2 A–D rule. 'Ghost per miss' is ghost dives avoided per dive above 0.04 missed. The recommended row combines the v2 A–D dive rule and A–C tow zone. Appendix D has the full comparisons."
hl_cell <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", 100 * x[1], 100 * x[2], 100 * x[3])
hl_ps <- function(v, m) c(ps(v, m), ps(v, m, "low"), ps(v, m, "high"))
hl_pd <- function(l, z, r, m) c(pdv(l, z, r, m), pdv(l, z, r, m, col = "low"), pdv(l, z, r, m, col = "high"))
hl_rd <- function(m) c(crd(m), crd(m, "low"), crd(m, "high"))
hl_row <- function(label, f) data.frame(
  Setting = label, `Dives skipped (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * f("dives_avoided_pct")[1]), `Ghost avoided (%)` = hl_cell(f("ghost_avoided_pct")),
  `>0.04 missed (%)` = hl_cell(f("high_missed_pct")), `Ghost per miss` = num(f("ghost_per_high_missed")[1], 1), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(rbind(
  hl_row("Site rule A–D, every dive", function(m) hl_ps(SR, m)),
  hl_row("Within-reef dive rule A–C", function(m) hl_pd("within-reef", "none", "A-C", m)),
  hl_row("Density-aware v2 dive rule A–D", function(m) hl_pd(V2, "none", "A-D", m)),
  hl_row("Same number at random", hl_rd),
  hl_row("Recommended: v2, dive rule A–D + tow zone A–C", function(m) hl_pd(V2, "A-C", "A-D", m))),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
```

### Surveillance {.unnumbered}

No new tow routes were designed or tested; surveillance options were assessed by thinning recorded surveys. In that comparison, habitat-only selection did not outperform evenly spaced tows (Appendix C). A narrower use of the ranking did better between full sweeps. On follow-up visits, the v2 A–C zone with season memory saved `r cri2("zone_saved_pct")` of tows and missed `r int(czb("zone_lost"))` dives above 0.04 over seven seasons. Skipping the same tows at other positions missed `r num(czb("shifted_lost"), 0)` (95% CI `r num(czb("shifted_lost", "low"), 0)`–`r num(czb("shifted_lost", "high"), 0)`). Blocks of nine tows on and three off saved `r p0(czb("block_saved_pct"))` and missed `r num(czb("block_lost"), 0)`. First visits of a season keep a full sweep.

### Seasonal products and exploration {.unnumbered}

The delivered ranking covers `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs, of which `r int(v2cl("all reefs", "density_v2_a_to_c"))` are in v2 classes A–C. Exploration zones shade all high-ranked habitat on `r int(length(unique(expz$reef_name)))` reefs that is outside designated sites and more than 150 m from tows of the last five seasons (@fig-2027). They show where search has rarely gone; the zones themselves have not been trialled.

## Preliminary larval dispersal patterns vary across the reef cluster {#sec-hydro-connectivity-results}

The larval-concentration maps showed uneven exposure to simulated larvae across `r int(lc_scope$sites)` sub-reef sites on `r int(lc_scope$reefs)` reefs during the 2022–23 spawning season. Persistent day-10 hotspots were concentrated on mid-shelf reefs south of the Lizard Island group, including Williamson, Mackay and Osterlund (@fig-larval-hotspots). The Lizard Island group was not a persistent hotspot at later larval ages. In the central part of the domain, later-age concentrations were generally higher on mid-shelf reefs than on Ribbon Reefs at similar latitudes. These one-season results remain sensitive to the domain boundary (Appendix E).

Colour shows the proportion of releases in which a sub-reef site ranked in the highest fifth of concentration within that release. The dashed box marks the enlarged area; grey shows land. This reformats concentration figure lc2 from the project analysis. High concentration does not by itself establish local retention, source strength or settlement.](../outputs/figures/fig28_larval_hotspot_persistence.png){#fig-larval-hotspots width="100%"}

## Historical COTS and coral dynamics provide a basis for testing control strategies {#sec-metacommunity-results}

The metacommunity model reproduced the broad sequence of historical irruption waves and coral decline and recovery on the four calibration reefs (@fig-metacommunity-cots-coral). Lizard Island's first (1990s) COTS peak remains too small, and the model exceeds observed densities during the build-up of the fifth wave on several reefs. That overshoot could understate the relative effect of contemporary culling. The paired culling trajectories show the model's response to recorded removals; they do not yet provide a validated estimate of the program's impact since 2012. Effort scenarios through 2050 demonstrate capability rather than likely outcomes.

![Historical COTS and coral dynamics on the calibration reefs. Left: manta-tow equivalents (dotted line: 0.22 COTS per tow). Right: hard coral cover, modelled relative to habitable area. Blue solid lines omit recorded culling; purple dashed lines apply it. Lines are five-seed means; darker bands span those seeds and lighter bands span all 65 parameter-test runs per culling state. These ranges are not confidence intervals. Black points show LTMP manta observations (coral bars: reported 95% intervals); orange diamonds show 9 m photo-transects. These are calibration and diagnostic comparisons.](../outputs/figures/fig22_metacommunity_cots_coral.png){#fig-metacommunity-cots-coral width="100%"}

On Martin and Linnet, outside the calibration score, the model placed past irruption peaks within two years, but did not consistently identify irruption years better than a no-model series. Three almost COTS-free outer reefs stayed below the irruption threshold only after a wave-exposure term was designed from them, so they are not validation (Appendix E).

# Discussion & Outputs

## Combining recent observations with habitat

The main tactical finding is that recent observations improve the order in which designated cull sites are searched, while habitat supplies an initial ordering where observations are absent. This extends the program's existing use of surveillance and crew knowledge [@fletcher2020strategy; @matthews2025intelligence]. The maps make that information more consistent and available across vessels. Their value lies in the comparison with random or simpler selection at the same effort, rather than in the reduction obtained simply by omitting sites.

Habitat alone ranked locations on the same reef weakly. This is compatible with reef-level distribution studies showing the importance of connectivity and conditions associated with irruption development [@matthews2020connectivity; @stewart2026hybrid]. Static terrain and coral habitat cannot describe the current stage of an irruption, recent removals or movement of aggregations. The recent-evidence ranking captures some of those changes, but also captures where crews chose to work. It should be interpreted as operational knowledge combined with habitat, rather than independent confirmation that a preferred location holds COTS.

The distinction matters most on rarely visited reefs and beyond designated sites. Prioritising repeated finds can continually direct effort towards the same footprint. Exploration zones provide a way to examine suitable habitat outside it, including lagoon patches and other places poorly covered by perimeter surveillance. Those zones remain hypotheses about where useful search could go. Records from new ground support investigating such gaps, but do not establish the detection yield of the proposed zones. Recording nil observations and effort will be as important as recording finds.

## Retention, surveillance and the cost of deferral

The A–D site rule shows what the ranking can do applied to every site, although the workflow below uses it more effectively. It retains approximately nine in ten observed high-density dives while selecting approximately four in five candidate cull sites. Most dives from 0.02 to 0.04 are also retained, preserving useful culling opportunities below the ecological target. Ghost and low-density dives form a larger share of the deferred set than under random site selection. Low-density avoidance is lower than random selection, however, and ghost-dive avoidance improves only slightly. The ranking also keeps more recorded dives overall at the same site count. The comparison supports protection of useful dives at equal candidate-site coverage; [Appendix C](#sec-ranking-alternatives) makes the additional comparison at equal recorded dive effort. Remaining high-density omissions require agreed tolerances and follow-up. The relevant target also depends on coral cover and the purpose of control [@plaganyi2020targets; @matthews2024protecting].

The separate manta estimate improves the interpretation of effort. Fewer cull sites selected does not translate directly into the same percentage fewer tows, because recorded segments cross site boundaries and include surveillance elsewhere. The geometry calculation preserves portions needed by retained sites and all portions outside designated sites, including nearby tows that do not intersect them. This conservatively limits the spatial accounting; further reductions outside polygons may be possible, but their feasibility and detection consequences are untested. The estimate does not show that crews would make the same dive decisions after associated manta evidence was removed, nor whether a shortened route saves vessel time.

Recent CPUE may improve prioritisation, but its extra gains were modest and varied among seasons. At matched retention it also kept slightly fewer intermediate dives than the current ranking. The experimental layer supports a direct field comparison rather than a replacement recommendation. Upper habitat percentiles did not strengthen the ranking in this test; this does not establish that real within-site hotspots are absent. Their value may depend on how the mapped habitat aligns with the areas crews actually search.

The retrospective tow comparison reinforces the need for coverage. Habitat-only selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning, although the latter is an analytical benchmark based on recorded surveys. Practical route planning must account for workability, travel, crew judgement and recent observations. A poor result for habitat-only thinning does not remove habitat's role in identifying additional places to search; it does rule out claiming that the habitat score alone supplies an improved exclusion rule.

Annual full surveys, pre-closure checks and revisits triggered by new evidence could detect populations initially deferred. They cannot guarantee that a missed aggregation will be found before coral is consumed. Later detections may also represent new population growth rather than an original false negative. An initial audit of deferred sites, together with dated follow-up and a maximum acceptable delay, is needed to distinguish these outcomes. Full-season effort must include those checks, repeat dives and exploration. January–February 2027 trials should test the ranking against normal crew planning before an annual saving is claimed.

## From rankings to an on-water workflow {#sec-workflow}

The workflow was not part of the original objectives, but it is the step that turns a site ranking into something a dive team can use on the day. A ranking says which sites are most likely to hold COTS; crews need to know which dive to make next, given what the morning's tows showed. Developing that translation with GBRMPA changed the result. Applied only where evidence was weak, the same ranking avoided more ghost and low-density dives, and missed fewer dives above 0.04, than applying it to every site (@tbl-operational-highlights).

@fig-workflow sets out the decisions for a reef visit. Open sites and strong manta evidence keep their current priority. The ranking enters at two points: where to tow on follow-up visits between full sweeps, and whether a site with only weak, negative or no tow evidence is worth a dive. Within classes A–D those dives remain the crew's decision, for example an adjacent site or ground not towed for a long time. Sites in class E wait for the next visit or the annual check. Crews can override any step when they see COTS or fresh feeding; recording why provides the evidence needed to refine the rules.

![Proposed decisions for a reef visit. Blue boxes are new steps; the rest is current practice. Strong evidence means a COTS sighting, two or more counted feeding scars, or scars recorded as common. The ranking is refreshed to each voyage's departure. The workflow was replayed on 2019–2026 records (Appendix D) and has not yet been trialled.](../outputs/figures/fig23_workflow_decision.png){#fig-workflow width="100%"}

The workflow also answers a question the program had already raised. GBRMPA's ad hoc analysis of feeding-scar evidence suggested that a two-scar trigger could avoid empty dives but risk missing sites above 0.04. The replay supports both parts of that concern. About `r p0(mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "ghost") / ptot$ghost)` of ghost dives followed weak-scar tows, yet a fixed two-scar trigger would have missed `r p0(ps("evidence rule: skip weak-scar dives", "high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04. Weak evidence is informative: `r p0(mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "high") / mzp("other: weak-scar tow", "dives"))` of weak-scar dives exceeded 0.04. The difficulty is therefore not the trigger itself, but choosing among weak-evidence sites, and the ranking supplies that choice from a site's habitat and recent history. Standardising the strong and weak evidence definitions across vessels is worthwhile in its own right.

The recommended settings are a management choice rather than a fixed optimum. The 5 November workshop moved the product from equal within-reef shares to density-aware classes, which are stricter, so the same cut-off skips more dives. Density-aware v2 at A–D avoided `r p0(crv("ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives for `r p1(crv("high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04 missed, with the most ghost dives avoided per miss of any rule tested. Moving the line to A–C would avoid `r p0(pdv(V2, "none", "A-C", "ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives but miss `r p1(pdv(V2, "none", "A-C", "high_missed_pct"))`. The tow zone has a different value: it saves boat time on follow-up visits but avoids few ghost dives. An A–C zone was preferred to A–B because it missed `r int(pdv(V2, "A-C", "none", "high_missed"))` rather than `r int(pdv(V2, "A-B", "none", "high_missed"))` dives above 0.04, for `r p0(pdv(V2, "A-C", "none", "tows_saved_follow_up_pct"))` rather than `r p0(pdv(V2, "A-B", "none", "tows_saved_follow_up_pct"))` of follow-up tows saved.

The replay has limits. It can only re-score dives that crews chose to make, and cannot show what undived sites held. A dive was counted as missed whenever its only strong tow was skipped, although crews might have dived there anyway. COTS at a skipped site remain until the next visit, so culled COTS forgone overstates the lasting loss, and tows saved count tows rather than vessel time. These limits frame the field trial. A median voyage held only `r int(cpv("flagged"))` dive`r if (cpv("flagged") == 1) "" else "s"` that the A–D rule would skip, so one trial voyage can test usability and towing time but not the dive rule's effect. Recording what the rule would have done on every voyage, with the ranking frozen at departure, would give a `r p0(cpt(25))` chance of detecting the expected difference after 25 voyages (Appendix D; [the operational impact pathway](#sec-monitoring)).

## Using connected population models for strategic decisions

The metacommunity strand addresses a different management scale: how culling on one reef affects COTS and coral there and on connected reefs. Reef-scale ecosystem models have already established the importance of comparing control strategies under interacting disturbances [@morello2014model; @condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative]. This prototype builds on COTSMod within a framework that can connect site-level habitat, population processes and intervention scenarios [@matthews2020cotsmod; @adriamethods2026]. Keeping the COTS equations in a reusable package also allows their use in other modelling frameworks.

The historical comparisons provide evidence that the framework can reproduce broad irruption cycles and respond to recorded removals. Martin and Linnet reefs, outside the calibration score, offer the most independent check, and they show right timing with uneven heights. Regional waves are shared among reefs, so correct timing is a modest test, and external larval supply came from a reef-level hindcast. The almost-COTS-free outer reefs initially showed false irruptions; the wave-exposure term that removed them was designed from those same records. Testing it on reefs not used in its design remains to be done. Peak sizes, densities between waves and the recent build-up depend on coral assumptions and the relationship between manta observations and true abundance. Recent cull and diver observations also informed the corrected larval inputs, so agreement with those observations is not independent validation. The excess simulated COTS carried into the near-term projections could affect the apparent benefit of culling. That sensitivity needs testing before estimates of coral protected are used in decisions.

The intended assessment of control since 2012 must compare paired histories beginning from the same population and coral state. Holding outside larval supply constant estimates the effect of control inside the model domain under unchanged outside conditions. A regional no-control history instead needs outside supply consistent with no control on those reefs. Those are different questions, and the existing reef-level irruption predictions do not supply the second counterfactual by themselves. Requested catches that exceed simulated availability must also remain visible, rather than being treated as successful removals.

For the fifth primary irruption wave, the useful comparison is among feasible allocations of present capacity, additional effort and rules for beginning or stopping control. A reef with little coral left to protect may still supply larvae to neighbours. Conversely, fewer COTS need not yield lasting local coral gains if heat stress or cyclones remove the spared coral. Scenarios must therefore follow larval export, downstream populations and coral recovery as well as local catches. The initial projections demonstrate this capability; they do not yet identify a preferred management strategy.

Larval-concentration hotspots provide a complementary regional signal, but concentration is not equivalent to settlement, local retention or source strength. Release-specific networks, distance-based comparisons and explicit tests of the northern boundary are needed before a hydrodynamic early-warning interpretation is supported. The metacommunity model still uses reef-level transport. Coupling the new habitat layers or fine-scale connections to intervention decisions is a subsequent test, rather than a completed integration. Appendices D and E give the field-assessment and scenario designs.

## Final project outputs

The outputs and their current evidence status are:

- GBR-wide 30 m habitat-suitability and search-priority layers, with a separate layer showing known aggregation locations and accompanying uncertainty products.
- The 2027 density-aware v2 cull-site ranking (classes A–E, from each site's own record and the reef's recent density), the product chosen for the 2027 trials, and shaded exploration zones, in CSV and KMZ formats, supported by forward evaluation. Within-reef and first density-aware classes and a recent-CPUE candidate are retained for comparison.
- A proposed on-water workflow for reef visits: decision steps, strong and weak evidence definitions, the A–D dive rule and A–C follow-up tow zone, replayed on 2020–2026 records with a one-voyage trial and season-long recording design; not yet trialled.
- Retrospective surveillance and cull-site comparisons, including the >0.04 retention assessment and separate conditional tow-effort estimates; operational deployment remains to be trialled.
- Lizard Island larval-concentration products and a reproducible COTS–coral metacommunity prototype with calibration diagnostics, checks on five reefs outside the calibration score and initial control scenarios; fine-scale network delivery and full validation remain open.
- This technical report and documented analysis workflows. Public repository registration, release identifiers and the final rights-holder information package require completion (Appendix A).

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Outcomes & Impact Pathway

## More efficient control through operational testing

The Work Plan selects CCIP Outcome 2, a more effective, efficient and scalable response to COTS irruptions, and Outcome 4, decisions informed by biophysical and predictive knowledge. The project contributes through explicit search priorities, measurable trade-offs and a platform for strategic comparisons. The outputs establish capability; reduced annual costs, improved detection and additional coral protection are intended outcomes that have not yet been demonstrated.

For Outcome 2, the immediate users are Control Program managers, vessel planners and dive teams. The ranking converts habitat and recent observations into a common site order that can be refreshed each season. This supports testing whether repeat searches at lower-priority sites can be deferred and whether some effort can be redirected to overlooked habitat. The 10–15% proposed reductions in surveillance searches and low-density or empty dives remain adoption targets. They require an agreed allowance for missed >0.04 dives, reliable follow-up coverage and a complete account of effort.

The proposed workflow ([Discussion](#sec-workflow)) is the intended vehicle for this test. It changes only dives on weak evidence and towing on follow-up visits, leaving open sites and strong manta evidence as now, so crews can adopt it without abandoning established triggers. It also gives GBRMPA's earlier scar-trigger question a tested answer that can be refined with field records.

Repeated GBRMPA meetings shaped delivery, including the choice to rank designated cull sites. This aligns the product with locations crews already recognise and record, while the exploration component addresses the limits of that register. The 5 November 2026 delivery workshop changed the product itself, leading to density-aware classes and shaded exploration zones. Product files can support Field Maps and COTS Dashboard workflows, but the report does not claim that either integration or routine uptake is complete.

## Co-interpretation with rights-holders and operators

The engagement described in Methods provides a direct pathway to testing usefulness with Traditional Owner operators. Malu's April visit and June follow-up also collected fine-scale observations for a future standalone Far Northern model. Those observations are an additional resource for subsequent work, rather than evidence validating the current GBR-wide ranking. Clear separation of the two avoids overstating where the delivered models have been tested.

January–February 2027 trials are planned aboard BPM in Cairns and with Malu in the Far Northern GBR and Torres Strait. The proposed design has two parts. On one voyage that includes at least three follow-up reefs, crews tow the zone first and the rest of the reef afterwards, so the same ground is towed once but any aggregation found only outside the zone becomes visible. Dives that the rule would skip are flagged and made last, so their outcomes are still recorded. That voyage tests usability, towing time and crew interpretation of low ranks. In parallel, freezing the ranking at each departure and scoring, from normal records, what the rule would have done tests the dive rule without changing operations; about 25 voyages are needed. Independent checks of deferred sites, annual and pre-closure checks, and all follow-up and exploration effort must enter the seasonal comparison. Agreement on monitoring ownership, reporting and the acceptable omission rate is needed before trial findings can support adoption. [TO CONFIRM: trial voyage, vessel and reporting arrangements agreed with GBRMPA and operators.]

## Predictive knowledge for cluster-scale management

For Outcome 4, the population model and dispersal analyses provide a framework for comparing control across connected reefs, including cases where local and downstream benefits differ. The intended users include GBRMPA planners and researchers developing control scenarios. The next steps are to resolve the recent population mismatch, complete independent checks and agree feasible effort and external-supply assumptions before estimating program impact since 2012 or recommending fifth-wave suppression strategies.

The delivery pathway therefore links documented consultation to field testing, repeatable evaluation and only then wider use. Suitable metadata, accessible product versions and clear limits are necessary for other researchers and managers to reproduce the comparisons. Data access and outstanding release requirements are stated below. No benefit is attributed to a model merely because it produces a map or a scenario trajectory.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Conclusions & Next Steps

This bridging project established a repeatable way to combine fine-scale habitat with recent operational evidence, rank every designated cull site and identify habitat beyond the usual search footprint. Recent observations supplied most of the tactical gain. Habitat alone discriminated weakly within reefs but provided coverage where current evidence was absent.

Applied to every site, the ranking retained more dives above 0.04 than random selection but avoided no more empty dives. Translated with GBRMPA into an on-water workflow that keeps open sites and strong manta evidence, and made density-aware after the 5 November 2026 delivery workshop, it avoided `r p0(crv("ghost_avoided_pct"))` of ghost dives while missing `r p1(crv("high_missed_pct"))` of dives above 0.04. The next operational step is the planned January–February 2027 trial of the density-aware v2 ranking, A–D dive rule and A–C tow zone: one voyage to test usability and towing time, with season-long recording to test the dive rule, an agreed omission allowance and checks of deferred sites.

At cluster scale, the COTS–coral prototype and larval-concentration products extend the capacity to ask where control could protect local and downstream coral. Full validation, the recent population-state mismatch, boundary supply and feasible effort must be resolved before historical program-impact estimates or fifth-wave strategies can guide management. Fine-scale hydrodynamic connections and habitat-informed control remain candidate extensions.

The most significant change is the availability of explicit, reproducible decisions and comparisons at the scale where crews search, together with a developing framework for their regional consequences. Rights-holder and operator co-interpretation, field trials and transparent data releases will determine how those capabilities become useful routine practice.

### Data and predictors {.unnumbered}

The habitat model fitted to manta observations used `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "tows"))` labelled tows in `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "reef_years"))` reef-years, including `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "strong_tows"))` with strong COTS evidence. Strong evidence meant a direct COTS sighting, at least two counted feeding scars, or scars recorded as “common” in legacy surveys. Strict negatives recorded neither COTS nor scars; weak single-scar records were excluded from model fitting. The observation archives included Control Program crews (2016 onward), the Reef Joint Field Management Program (2012 onward) and AIMS LTMP (1992 onward), as specified by the author. SALAD [@pratchett2022salad] and RHIS [@beeden2014rhis] observations contributed to the joint habitat model. ReefScan imagery [@bainbridge2024reefscan] supplied a separate presence-only check in script 10 and was not a fitted response in the delivered joint model.

Exactly 0.02 CPUE counts as positive under the original response and as intermediate in the >0.04 evaluation; exactly 0.04 is also intermediate. Predictors were assembled on a 30 m grid in GDA2020 / MGA zone 55 (@tbl-predictors). ReefGuide coverage was reduced in some deeper areas, particularly beyond about 15–20 m.

| Code | Layer | Stack |
|---|---|---|
| DEM | Depth | Clean |
| SLO | Slope | Clean |
| EAST, NORTH | Eastness, northness (aspect) | Clean |
| BPI | Bathymetric position index | Clean |
| VRM | Vector ruggedness measure | Clean |
| SVF | Sky-view factor | Clean |
| HCU, VCU | Horizontal and vertical curvature | Clean |
| AhyaD, Aspat, Aten | Coral habitat suitability for three *Acropora* taxa | Clean |
| RG_bathy, RG_slope | ReefGuide bathymetry and slope | ReefGuide |
| RG_turbid | ReefGuide turbidity | ReefGuide |
| RG_waves_Hs, RG_waves_Tp | ReefGuide significant wave height and wave period | ReefGuide |

: Predictor codes. The terrain and coral-habitat surfaces follow @guillaume2025coral; additional layers were accessed through ReefGuide [@reefguide2026]. GBR10 mapping sources are @gbrmpabathymetry2021, @gbrmpageomorphic2021 and @roelfsema2021shallow. [TO CONFIRM: exact predictor product versions and resampling methods.] {#tbl-predictors}

### Habitat models and mapped layers {.unnumbered}

The clean + year model used gradient-boosted trees [XGBoost; @chen2016xgboost] to predict the problematic-density indicator from the clean stack and survey year. The RG + year model added the five ReefGuide predictors. These cull-trained models learned from locations selected by crews, often following manta evidence, so their scores reflect the program's sampling footprint as well as habitat. The operational refits used 1,500 boosting rounds, a learning rate of 0.00137382379588326, maximum tree depth 5, minimum child weight 20 and gamma $10^{-10}$, retaining the archived hyperparameters. These settings were not retuned on the evaluation reefs.

The primary search-planning layer used RG + year where available and clean + year elsewhere, calibrated onto the RG probability scale before combining them. Each 30 m cell was then ranked within its reef polygon, with map priority classes for the top 10%, 10–20% and 20–30%. RG + year covered `r p0(pick(lcov, layer_id = "legacy_rg_year2026", col = "fraction"))` of the reef-polygon support cells used in the coverage analysis. Of the mapped reefs, `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "RG only"))` used RG alone, `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "mixed"))` mixed the two sources and `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "clean fallback only"))` used the clean fallback alone.

Manta-trained XGBoost models used the RG stack and the same boosting settings. Predictor values were averaged along each tow. A model with survey year was compared with a model designed specifically to rank locations within reef-years. For the latter, the logit of the reef-year's strong-tow proportion, with a half-count correction, entered training as a fixed offset and survey year was omitted. The offset was omitted when predicting relative habitat scores because it was constant within a reef-year. The resulting map represents relative log-odds, not an annual occurrence probability. The cull-trained and manta-trained ranks were also compared as an average rank and as separate terms in the evidence model.

The hierarchical model of species communities [HMSC; @ovaskainen2017hmsc; @tikhonov2020hmsc] related cull, SALAD and RHIS responses jointly to habitat at 120 m, conditional on an active reef-year, and supplied explanatory habitat effects and uncertainty. Production fits used four chains, each retaining 1,000 samples at thinning 30 after 5,000 transient iterations. All components passed the convergence gates (smallest effective sample size `r int(min(hsum$min_ess))`, against a minimum of 400; largest upper potential scale reduction factor `r a3(max(hsum$max_psrf_upper))`, against a maximum of 1.1).

An additional layer represented known aggregation sites using a Gaussian kernel of the problematic rate in earlier active cull site-years (σ = 500 m). Its rate *H* and evidence weight *W* updated the HMSC habitat probability *p* as (κ*p* + *WH*)/(κ + *W*), with κ = 2 for the fixed-setting comparison. History and dive effort were interpreted as records of past finds and crew targeting, rather than independent habitat evidence.

### How habitat and recent observations determine a cull-site rank {.unnumbered}

A site's score is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_i &= \beta_0+\beta_H H_i+\beta_P P_i+\beta_Q Q_i+\beta_R R_i\\
&\quad+\beta_E\log(1+E_i)+\beta_M\log(1+M_i)+\beta_T\log(1+T_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $H_i$ is the mean habitat score inside site $i$, ranked among designated sites on its reef. $P_i$ records whether any recent dive there reached CPUE ≥0.02; $Q_i$ records a searched site where none did. $R_i$ is the distance-weighted proportion of nearby dives reaching ≥0.02; $E_i$ is the weighted count of dives. $M_i$ and $T_i$ are weighted counts of strong-evidence and all nearby manta tows. Nearby records receive decreasing weights out to 900 m. Coefficients ($\beta$) were estimated jointly from dive outcomes at ≥0.02, rather than assigned as rules. All sites were ordered by decreasing score on each reef. Appendix B gives the distance equation, coefficients, missing-data treatment and priority classes.

Here $H_i$ is the mean habitat score inside site $i$, ranked among designated sites on its reef. $P_i$ records whether any recent dive there reached CPUE ≥0.02; $Q_i$ records a searched site where none did. $R_i$ is the distance-weighted proportion of nearby dives reaching ≥0.02; $E_i$ is the weighted count of dives. $M_i$ and $T_i$ are weighted counts of strong-evidence and all nearby manta tows. The fitted response was whether a dive reached CPUE ≥0.02; reassessment at >0.04 changed the evaluation target, not this model. The habitat term $H_i$ was the mean deployed habitat score over a site's polygon, converted to a percentile among designated sites on the reef. A missing habitat rank was replaced by 0.5. The operational product used the cull-trained habitat layer with its full-extent fallback, without a second manta-habitat term.

Recent dive and tow records were represented at dive coordinates and tow midpoints. Missing dive coordinates used a representative point inside the matched site. For site $i$ and nearby record $j$, the spatial weight was:

$$
w_{ij}=\begin{cases}
\exp\left[-d_{ij}^{2}/\{2(300\,\mathrm{m})^{2}\}\right], & d_{ij}\leq900\,\mathrm{m},\\
0, & d_{ij}>900\,\mathrm{m}.
\end{cases}
$$

Distances were measured from the site's representative interior point in GDA2020 / MGA zone 55. The calculation considered at most the 400 nearest records in each data stream. $E_i=\sum_j w_{ij}$ was the weighted number of dive records, not minutes of bottom time. $R_i=\sum_j w_{ij}y_j/E_i$, where $y_j=1$ for CPUE ≥0.02, was their weighted positive proportion. The analogous tow sums supplied $T_i$ for all records and $M_i$ for strong evidence (a direct COTS sighting, multiple counted scars or legacy common scars). Searches with no strong evidence contributed to effort but not to the positive sum. There was no additional age weighting within the evidence window.

The direct-site indicators were $P_i=1$ if any recent dive assigned to that site reached ≥0.02, and $Q_i=1$ if the site was dived but none reached that threshold. Both were zero for an undived site. Where no nearby dives were available, $R_i$ and $E_i$ were zero; absent tows gave $M_i=T_i=0$. With no recent evidence, the score therefore reduced to the intercept plus habitat term. No evidence was treated differently from a searched site with a quiet result.

The coefficients were estimated jointly by logistic regression. They are conditional associations, not independent bonuses or penalties. @tbl-ranking-coefficients records the final 2027 coefficients; the forward evaluation estimated a different coefficient set using only years preceding each test year.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ranking-coefficients
#| tbl-cap: "Coefficients used in the 2027 cull-site score, fitted to the archived ≥0.02 dive response. Inputs and transformations match the score equation above. These coefficients describe the deployed fit, not the separately fitted forward-validation years."
rank_terms <- c("(Intercept)","habitat","site_problematic_prev","site_quiet_prev","cull_rate","log_cull_effort","log_manta_strong","log_manta_effort")
stopifnot(identical(as.character(src$term),rank_terms))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Input=c("Intercept","Within-reef habitat rank","Any ≥0.02 dive at this site","Dived here, none ≥0.02","Nearby ≥0.02 dive proportion","log(1 + weighted dive count)","log(1 + weighted strong tow count)","log(1 + weighted total tow count)"),
 Symbol=c("β₀","βH","βP","βQ","βR","βE","βM","βT"),Coefficient=num(src$estimate,3),check.names=FALSE),row.names=FALSE)
```

The logistic transform $p_i=1/(1+\exp[-s_i])$ expresses the fitted probability of a ≥0.02 outcome conditional on diving there. Rankings use $s_i$, so the transform does not change their order. This is not a probability of an irruption or of presence at an unvisited site. In the deployed product, sites are sorted from highest to lowest score on each reef, using higher cull-habitat rank to break score ties. Descending rank divided by the reef's site count defines A (≤0.2), B (>0.2 to 0.5), C (>0.5 to 0.66), D (>0.66 to 0.8) and E (>0.8); retaining A–D selects floor(0.8 × site count). Until 2 November 2026 the product had four classes, with C covering 0.5 to 0.8 and D the bottom 20%; C was split at 0.66 so that the workflow's dive rule could use the top two-thirds. Scores and ranks were unchanged, and earlier "A–C" results in review copies correspond to A–D here. Pop-up evidence labels describe the records; they do not override the fitted score. Historical evaluation retains the archived random tie order.

For validation, prior evidence came from the preceding calendar season. The 2027 product instead used the latest complete 365-day window, 1 June 2025–31 May 2026, and coefficients fitted on `r int(src$training_dives[1])` dives from `r src$training_years[1]`. The search tool is therefore a habitat ranking updated with both positive and negative operational evidence, and its effort terms also encode where crews chose to work.

### Evaluation design {.unnumbered}

Operational discrimination was measured among locations on the same reef in the same year. Within reef-year AUC compared positive and negative locations only within those groups; an AUC of 0.5 indicated no discrimination. Top-20% lift was the share of positives in the highest-ranked fifth divided by 0.2. These metrics were supplemented by the outcomes retained when effort was reduced.

For operational habitat comparisons, reefs were assigned to five folds and every reef was scored by a model refitted without any reefs in its fold [@roberts2017cv]. The pipeline calls this leave-reef-out validation; it is grouped five-fold validation, rather than one refit per reef. In the season-by-season test, the evidence regression for each test year from 2019 to 2026 was fitted only on earlier dive outcomes, while its habitat covariates were the reef-held-out ranks, whose fits were not restricted to earlier years. Rankings were compared at matched retention, because evidence could move both problematic and low-density dives upwards. The >0.04 reassessment rescored the saved rankings without refitting.

Manta aggregations were connected groups of strong-evidence tow midpoints linked within 500 m in a survey (reef and date); successive links could join a group wider than 500 m. The principal aggregation analysis required at least two strong tows, with isolated records examined separately. Surveys required at least five scored tows and some strong evidence. An aggregation was retained if at least one of its tows was kept. This measured retention of observed aggregation evidence under retrospective thinning.

Each thinning strategy kept the same number of tows per survey, over retained shares from 90% to 30%. Random thinning used the exact hypergeometric expectation; systematic thinning kept evenly spaced positions, averaged over 20 starting offsets. Recorded tow order was unavailable, so sequence was approximated by bearing from the survey centre.

The manta-effort estimate split straight tow segments at designated-site boundaries. A portion could be deferred only if it lay within designated sites and all sites sharing it were deferred; parts outside designated sites remained surveyed. The whole-tow metric counted only segments entirely deferred. These estimates describe spatial scope for reducing recorded surveillance, conditional on still diving selected sites; no tow-to-dive detection model, route feasibility or vessel-time saving was inferred.

Uncertainty intervals used paired bootstrap resamples of reef-years for tow and cull metrics, or surveys for aggregation retention. Operational spatial comparisons used 500 resamples; the season-by-season site-ranking test used 200. The same resampled units were used across scores to preserve paired comparisons.

### Exploration zones {.unnumbered}

Exploration zones were drawn from 30 m cells 0.5–16 m deep, more than 100 m from designated cull sites and more than 150 m from manta tows in the preceding five seasons. Habitat was the mean of the primary-layer and manta-model percentiles, with the primary layer alone where manta scores were missing. It was smoothed with a 150 m moving mean (5 × 5 cells) and re-ranked within the reef. Eligible cells in the reef's top 40, 30, 20 and 10% formed four nested bands. Each band's outline was closed and opened by 30 m, smoothed, cleared of holes smaller than 0.5 ha, clipped to the reef outside cull sites, and stripped of pieces smaller than 0.5 ha. An earlier version picked up to ten discrete areas per reef; those areas did not differ clearly from the ground around them, because the habitat layers rank places within a reef only weakly. The zones instead show all rarely searched ground that looks like habitat, shaded darker where habitat ranks higher.

### Limits of the search evaluation {.unnumbered}

The search evaluation used outcomes from dives crews chose to make. It cannot establish densities at never-dived sites or the consequences of changing crew behaviour. Reefs without recent observations depend mainly on habitat, where discrimination is weak. Spatially held-out habitat scores reduce bias from scoring a reef with its own training data, but the season-by-season evidence test did not also restrict the habitat fits to preceding years. The evidence regression was tested forward in time; the entire combined modelling process was not a fully prospective forecast.

Spatial coverage also limits interpretation. The primary habitat layer joins models with different predictor coverage, and their rankings differ near that boundary. The explanatory joint habitat model relies heavily on fallback predictors in some regions. Values from the manta-trained model away from tow paths are extrapolations, including in parts of the exploration zones. The retrospective thinning result also depends on an inferred order around the reef, which may be less suitable for surveys that do not follow the perimeter. None of the proposed 2027 products has yet demonstrated its performance in a field trial.
